headline: Highest risk is prompt-injection/data-flow via Continue’s filesystem and MCP tooling; the pair otherwise has limited direct conflict because spring-integration-samples is non-runnable and network-isolated.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and can use MCP/tool calls, so malicious content in shared files or outputs could influence it. spring-integration-samples is a code sample repo, so if its contents are opened in the same workspace, Continue may ingest attacker-controlled text. The pair lacks a documented shared channel, so this is inferred from Continue’s default surfaces.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace files or copied snippets
IF Continue parses repository text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable MCP for the session
Open the sample repo in a separate workspace
Review file contents before feeding them to Continue
Use read-only access for the sample repo
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for tool inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue can read workspace files and has broad network egress, but spring-integration-samples reports no data classes touched and no network egress. The main leakage path is local workspace exposure rather than a documented exfiltration route, so blast radius is limited unless sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace
IF Continue is pointed at those files during a session
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Use a throwaway repo clone for testing
Restrict Continue to non-sensitive folders
Rotate any exposed credentials immediately
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while spring-integration-samples is a non-runnable sample repo with no write capabilities or mutable shared state documented. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely; the only plausible conflict is if both are pointed at the same files, which is an unusual setup.
conditions: IF both agents are granted write access to the same directory
IF an external orchestrator lets both mutate shared files concurrently
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Make the sample repo read-only
Serialize edits through one agent at a time
Avoid concurrent runs on the same checkout
requires-engineering: add file-locking in the orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or edits from repository context, and a downstream consumer could treat those outputs as authoritative. spring-integration-samples is a sample repository, so if its content is used as input to Continue, errors can propagate into generated artifacts. No verification step is documented between them, so the interaction is plausible in default coding workflows.
conditions: IF Continue’s output is copied into downstream code or configuration
IF the sample repository content is used as authoritative input without review
mitigations: Require human review before applying edits
Compare generated output against source docs
Limit Continue to suggestion-only mode
Test changes in a disposable branch
requires-engineering: add automated validation gates

E_compliance.rationale: Continue handles model-provider API keys and may send workspace content to a chosen provider, while spring-integration-samples is open-source and does not declare sensitive-data handling. There is no explicit residency or regulated-data mismatch in the profiles, so compliance risk is limited to accidental exposure if operators place regulated data in the workspace.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF Continue is configured to send that content to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in the repo
Use a local model provider
Review provider retention settings
Document data-handling boundaries
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing
